title: Estimates of natural frequencies for nuclear vibration, and an assessment of the feasibility of selective ultrasound ablation of cancer cells
journal: Journal of the Mechanical Behavior of Biomedical Materials
model_context: multiple cancerous and non-cancerous cell types / brain regions
primary_method: cell/nuclear size + effective indentation modulus + theoretical model
bottom_line: Potential nuclear natural-frequency differences on the order of tens of kHz were estimated for certain cancerous vs non-cancerous cells; selective ultrasound ablation has not yet been achieved.
relevance: Directly supports the project question, but does not validate a GBM treatment frequency.
verification_notes: Verified against PubMed primary-paper abstract. Exact cell-type-specific frequencies were not available in the abstract and are not entered as verified numeric values.

title: Single-cell mechanical assay unveils viscoelastic similarities in normal and neoplastic brain cells
model_context: U87 human GBM vs immortalized human astrocytes
primary_method: fluid shear stress + imaging + generalized Maxwell model
bottom_line: U87 GBM and immortalized human astrocytes showed no statistically significant differences in nuclear or cytoplasmic stiffness, viscosity, or relaxation time under the tested shear assay.
relevance: Important challenge to a simple universal GBM-vs-healthy stiffness-separation assumption.
verification_notes: Verified against full text, including Table 1 and Results. Values below are mean ± SEM.

title: Aligned Nanotopography Promotes a Migratory State in Glioblastoma Multiforme Tumor Cells
model_context: human U87MG/A172/BT145 GBM vs primary rat astrocytes
primary_method: atomic force microscopy + traction force microscopy
bottom_line: GBM tumor cells were significantly softer than primary astrocytes; more invasive GBM initiating cells were softer still.
relevance: Strong mechanical contrast in vitro, but comparator is cross-species and substrate/context dependent.
verification_notes: Verified against open full text. Exact AFM stiffness values are included below.

title: Compression stiffening of brain and its effect on mechanosensing by glioma cells
model_context: LN229 glioma / normal astrocytes / human glioma tissue / normal brain tissue
bottom_line: Human glioma tissue had elastic moduli on the order of 200 Pa and was indistinguishable from normal brain without compression, but glioma tissue stiffened more strongly under compression; normal astrocytes were stiffer than glioma cells in vitro.
relevance: Shows that cell-scale and tissue-scale mechanics can give different answers and depend on mechanical state.
verification_notes: Verified against PubMed and PMC full text. The ~200 Pa tissue statement is an order-of-magnitude result, not entered as a precise group mean.

title: Nanomechanics and Histopathology as Diagnostic Tools to Characterize Freshly Removed Human Brain Tumors
model_context: human healthy brain / tissue adjacent to GBM / GBM tissue
bottom_line: Fresh GBM tissue was highly mechanically heterogeneous and, in the sampled ex vivo tissue, approximately three- to fourfold stiffer than healthy or adjacent tissue; healthy and adjacent tissue means were 66.4 ± 39.2 Pa and 47.2 ± 21.9 Pa.
relevance: Strong evidence of tissue-scale mechanical heterogeneity, but not the same thing as isolated-cell resonance.
evidence_direction: supports tissue mechanical contrast and heterogeneity
verification_notes: Verified against open full text. Exact overall GBM mean was not safely recoverable from the accessible text, so only directly visible healthy/adjacent values are seeded.

title: Multiscale rheology of glioma cells
model_context: human glioma cells of different grades
bottom_line: Grade IV GBM cells were softer than grade III astrocytoma cells in whole-cell measurements but stiffer at the intracellular scale, demonstrating scale-dependent mechanical behavior.
relevance: Shows why one scalar stiffness value may be inadequate for frequency modeling.
verification_notes: Verified against PubMed primary-paper abstract; no matched healthy comparator.

title: The glioblastoma biomechanical landscape: A systematic review of magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) of brain tumors and healthy brain
model_context: human GBM / healthy brain, plus animal models
bottom_line: Pooled human GBM measurements suggested overall stiffness similar to surrounding healthy brain, whereas mouse GBM tended to appear softer than brain tissue.
relevance: Direct warning that in vivo human tissue mechanics may not match AFM/in-vitro assumptions.

title: Microscale mechanical properties of brain tumor characterized by atomic force microscopy: implications for delineation of glioblastoma margin
bottom_line: GBM tissue showed pronounced spatial mechanical heterogeneity; Young’s modulus varied across tumor center and margins, with the inner margin displaying the strongest heterogeneity.
relevance: Strong evidence that GBM cannot be represented by one mechanical number.
verification_notes: Verified against PubMed primary-paper abstract. Exact GBM-region values are included below; healthy mouse values were not stated in the abstract.

title: Compressible viscoelasticity of cell membranes determined by gigahertz-frequency acoustic vibrations
model_context: human LN-18 GBM vs mouse bEnd.3 brain endothelial cells
primary_method: GHz acoustic vibration damping of gold nanoplates + viscoelastic model
bottom_line: Measured membrane viscosity was about threefold lower in LN-18 GBM cells than in bEnd.3 cells.
relevance: Direct acoustic/viscoelastic differentiation evidence, but at GHz frequencies and with a cross-species, non-astrocyte comparator.
evidence_direction: supports acoustic mechanical differentiation, with major context caveats
verification_notes: Verified against PubMed full record/figures. Not directly transferable to kHz therapeutic ultrasound.

title: The Biomechanics of Glioblastoma: Why Glioblastoma Models and Clinical Reality Diverge
bottom_line: Preclinical in-vitro/ex-vivo studies often report increased GB stiffness, whereas clinical in-vivo studies often report decreased stiffness; method, scale, sample preparation, edema, necrosis and confinement contribute to the discrepancy.
relevance: Explains why a literature engine must harmonize method and scale rather than pool all stiffness values.
